source.title: Do Models See in Line with Human Vision? Probing the Correspondence Between LVLM Representations and EEG Signals
source.authors: Xin Xiao; Yang Lei; Haoyang Zeng; Xiao Sun; Xinyi Jiang; Yu Tian; Hao Wu; Kaiwen Wei; Jiang Zhong

record.tranche_reason: The study measures LVLM-to-human-EEG correspondence, not similarity or convergence between independently trained models. Its findings therefore do not test the listed versions of the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports EEG-prediction correlations, layer/time patterns, category differences, and capability associations. These concern model-to-brain correspondence rather than model-to-model convergence; the rows below record the Table 1 Pearson results as related findings, with versions set to none. Other metrics are reported and compared in Table 1, but are not separate rows here because they measure the same out-of-version brain-alignment finding.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well LVLM image features predict human EEG responses (ridge regression, RSA, CKA). It reports no similarity between independently trained models and no image–caption alignment across vision and language models. Model-to-brain alignment is a related but different construct, so it does not test any version. The Platonic hypothesis is not even cited.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that LVLMs align significantly with EEG, with intermediate layers (8–16) peaking at 100–300 ms. They find that architecture outweighs parameter scaling (3.4×), that LVLMs beat vision-only ViTs, and that alignment correlates with benchmark performance.
record.recipe_differences: Measures model-to-EEG prediction and representational correspondence, rather than similarity between independently trained models.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that EEG correspondence varies across Pearson, Spearman, CKA, RSA, and Kendall measures (Appendix A.5); it also reports input-configuration differences, including reduced alignment for a black image with a caption (Table 2). These are sensitivities of brain alignment, not model-to-model convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: All 32 LVLMs' image features predict THINGS-EEG responses above a random baseline (Pearson ~0.21–0.26). Alignment depends more on architecture or family than on scale: InternVL3.5 2B→38B gains 1.6 points, while the family gap is about 5.5 points. Alignment correlates with OpenCompass benchmark scores (avg R²=0.61).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-to-brain (EEG) alignment of LVLM visual features rises with capability, but not consistently with parameter scale. This is a brain-alignment analogue of convergence, not model-to-model convergence.

record.problems: The study tests correspondence to EEG rather than convergence between models. The authors note limited visual stimuli, EEG's limited spatial resolution, and lack of evaluation on closed-source LVLMs. Table 1 provides means and standard deviations across subjects; no model-to-model similarity measurements are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's additional Spearman, CKA, RSA, and Kendall values are omitted because they report the same out-of-version model-to-EEG correspondence as the retained Pearson rows. Also omitted are layer/time and category results, the Table 2 input-configuration results, and benchmark-performance correlations; none measures a listed version of model-to-model convergence.

untested.parts: Model-to-model alignment as a function of scale or capability. Only model-to-EEG alignment versus scale and benchmark score is reported.
Vision–language alignment on paired image–caption data.
Mapping or stitching between models. Ridge maps go from model to EEG only.
Recurring features or circuits across models.
Metric and input dependence of model-to-model convergence. Metric sensitivity is shown only for model-to-EEG alignment.
Plateau or shared-data explanations of model-to-model alignment.

record.verdict_notes: Classified as T6/discusses: model-to-brain correspondence only. Benchmark scores in Figure 6 come from the OpenCompass leaderboard, not the authors' own runs. Several appendix model descriptions appear inaccurate (e.g., DeepSeek-VL2 described as MobileViT-based, while Table 3 lists SigLIP-400M); this does not affect the verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Whether independently trained models' representations become more aligned with one another as model size or capability increases.
Whether representations of paired images and captions from vision and language models align more as both models improve.
Whether same-architecture models trained from different initializations share features or subspaces.
Whether representations can be mapped, stitched, or otherwise transferred between models.
Whether interpretable features or circuits recur across models.
Whether measured model-to-model convergence changes with similarity metrics, settings, or input distributions.
Whether model-to-model alignment plateaus or is explained by shared data or objectives.

relation.reason: It discusses representational correspondence through model–brain alignment, without testing or operationally using model-to-model convergence.

tranche.reason: The study measures model-to-human EEG correspondence, a related construct that neither tests nor uses any listed version of convergence between independently trained models.

source_check.notes: All sampled values and uncertainties match Table 1; uncertainties are standard deviations across subjects. Scaling, metric and input effects concern EEG correspondence and do not establish results on V1–V7.
